blocks.text: 4.5.4 Scheduling Vegetation Crews Across Circuits

This lesson puts the module together into the schedule GridCap's vegetation manager actually needs. Twelve jobs across four regions, a pool of three crews with one held back for storm duty in weeks 12 to 15, circuit clears that must sit inside their region's outage windows, one outage per region at a time: all of lesson 4.5.2's rules at once. And now a due week for every job, with a weight that says how much it matters.

Why due weeks? Trees keep growing during the season. A circuit whose conductors are already close to the canopy (GridCap's asset-health model gives it a short remaining useful life) carries a higher chance of a tree contact, an outage or a fire for every week its trim waits. `season.py` turns that into two numbers per job (GridCap and these rules are fictional):

items: the **due week** $`\delta_j`$: week 6 if the asset's remaining useful life is 2 years or less, week 12 if it is 15 or less, week 20 otherwise;
the **weight** $`w_j`$: the asset's consequence of failure divided by 100, read as $k of risk carried for every week the job finishes after its due week.

blocks.text: The makespan of lessons 4.5.1 and 4.5.2 is blind to all of this. The manager's question is "which schedule carries the least risk?", and the answer is a different objective: the **risk-weighted lateness**, the sum over jobs of weight times weeks late.
Due Weeks as Hard Rules Make the Season Infeasible
The first idea is to make every due week a rule, $`s_j + d_j \le \delta_j`$:

hard = build(season, **RULES)
for j in season:
    hard.model.add(hard.end(j.jid) <= j.due)
print("every due week as a hard rule:", solve(hard.model)[1])
every due week as a hard rule: INFEASIBLE

`INFEASIBLE` means CP-SAT proved that no schedule meets every rule. Here you can see why by hand. Five jobs are due at week 6: P004 (6 weeks, 1 crew), P006 (4 weeks, 2 crews), P008 (6 weeks, 1 crew), P011 (4 weeks, 1 crew) and P012 (6 weeks, 2 crews). They need $`6 + 8 + 6 + 4 + 12 = 36`$ crew-weeks before week 6, and three crews supply 18. No ordering can fix that. A due week that cannot always be met is not a rule but a wish, and a wish belongs in the objective, where it can be traded against other wishes.
Lateness Is max(0, end − due), and Its Weight Is the Risk Carried
The **lateness** of job $`j`$ is how many weeks it finishes after its due week, and 0 if it finishes on time or early:
L_j = \max\big(0,\; s_j + d_j - \delta_j\big)

The floor at 0 matters: finishing early earns nothing. Without it, a job that ends three weeks early would count $`-3`$ and pay for another job's lateness, which is not how risk works. CP-SAT writes the max directly with `add_max_equality`, as the makespan was written, and the objective weights each lateness by its job's risk:
\min \; \sum_{j \in J} w_j\, L_j

`add_max_equality` makes $`L_j`$ *equal* to the max, so the value you read back is the lateness itself. A MIP writes the same objective with two rows, $`L_j \ge 0`$ and $`L_j \ge s_j + d_j - \delta_j`$, and lets the minimization push $`L_j`$ down onto the larger of the two; that also works here, because a smaller $`L_j`$ always lowers the objective. The equality is simply exact whatever the objective.
`season_lateness.py` builds the full season (every rule of lesson 4.5.2) with this objective:

s = build(season, **RULES)
minimize_lateness(s)
solver, status = solve(s.model)
best = starts(s, solver)

least risk: OPTIMAL, risk-weighted lateness $360k, makespan 24
  P004 Plains trim  crews 1  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P008 Ridge  clear crews 1  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P011 Coast  trim  crews 1  weeks  0- 3  due  6
  P015 Coast  clear crews 1  weeks  4- 5  due 12
  P010 Valley clear crews 1  weeks  6- 9  due 12
  P012 Coast  widen crews 2  weeks  6-11  due  6  late 6 x 22
  P003 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 10-11  due 20
  P035 Ridge  widen crews 2  weeks 12-17  due 20
  P014 Coast  trim  crews 1  weeks 16-17  due 20
  P018 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 18-23  due 20  late 4 x 30
  P020 Ridge  widen crews 2  weeks 18-19  due 20
  P006 Valley widen crews 2  weeks 20-23  due  6  late 18 x 6
rules broken: none

Three jobs are late: P012 by 6 weeks at $22k a week, P018 by 4 at $30k, and P006 by 18 at $6k. $`132 + 120 + 108 = 360`$, the objective. Compare the two late corridors due at week 6. P006, with the lowest weight of the season ($6k a week), is the job left to the very end of the season, 18 weeks late. P012, at $22k, starts at week 6: in weeks 0 to 5 the three crews are on P004, P008 and P011 (also due at week 6) and P015, which leaves no week with the two crews P012 needs. `OPTIMAL` says that no schedule keeping every rule carries less than $360k, so any other way of sharing out the lateness costs at least as much.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Shortest Season Is Not the Safest One
The same rules with the makespan objective, and the risk of the schedule it returns, computed afterwards from its starts:

fast = build(season, **RULES)
minimize_makespan(fast)
solver, status = solve(fast.model)
quick = starts(fast, solver)
print(f"shortest season: {status}, makespan {solver.value(fast.makespan)}, "
      f"risk-weighted lateness ${risk(season, quick)}k")
shortest season: OPTIMAL, makespan 24, risk-weighted lateness $1038k

Both schedules end at week 24, and the makespan objective cannot tell them apart. Their risk differs almost threefold: $1,038k against $360k. Lesson 4.5.1 noted that, for one crew, any order of the jobs gave the same makespan; with due weeks the order is the whole question, and only an objective that sees the due weeks can answer it.

This is a general lesson about objectives, not about scheduling. An objective is a statement of what the planner values, and the solver optimizes exactly that and nothing else. Two optimal schedules for two objectives can share every rule and differ in everything the planner cares about. When a schedule looks wrong, ask first whether the objective says what was meant. When the planners care about both, rank them: first the least risk, then, among schedules with that risk, the shortest season. That is a prioritized objective, which lesson 4.3.2 builds in MathOpt with `add_auxiliary_objective`. Lesson 8.2.1, later in the course, treats such hierarchies of objectives in depth.
A Checker Written From the Rules Proves the Schedule

How do you know the model says what the planners said? Write the rules a second time, in plain Python, as a function that takes a schedule and lists every rule it breaks, and run it on what the solver returns. The checker shares no code with the model: it reads the same data, and nothing else.

(The function goes on with the one-outage-per-region rule, pair by pair.) It is slow and obvious on purpose: a loop over weeks, a sum per week, a test per rule, each written the way the planner says it. `season_lateness.py` already printed its verdict on the least-risk schedule, `rules broken: none`. A checker earns its keep when it can fail, so `check_demo.py` also runs it on two hand edits of the solver's schedule:

solver's schedule: risk $360k, rules broken: none
P015 moved to week 9: risk $360k
   P015 is not inside one Coast outage window (weeks 9-10)
   week 9: 4 crews at work, 3 available
   week 10: 4 crews at work, 3 available
P003 moved to week 8: risk $360k
   week 8: 4 crews at work, 3 available
   week 9: 4 crews at work, 3 available
   P003 and P010 de-energize Valley circuits at the same time

Each edit breaks rules the risk alone would never show: the risk is the same $360k, since neither job is late. In a test suite (the section 12 lesson *Unit-testing one constraint at a time* builds one), the checker runs on every schedule the model returns, for every instance, so a model change that quietly drops a rule fails the build instead of reaching a planner.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Named Crews Come From Handing Out Free Crews in Start Order

The cumulative constraint promises that no week needs more crews than there are. It does not say *which* crew does which job, and a crew foreman needs a name on the work order. Can every pool schedule be turned into named crews? Yes, and with a simple rule: go through the jobs (and the standby) in order of start week, and give each the crews that are free at its start.

Why does it never run short? Think of a job that needs $`k`$ crews as $`k`$ copies of the same interval. At the moment a job starts, the crews still busy are exactly those on jobs that started earlier and have not ended, and the cumulative constraint says those, plus this job's demand, fit in the pool. So enough crews are free. (This is the classic result that intervals can be coloured with as many colours as the most of them that overlap at one time.) Note what makes it work: the jobs are handed out in start order. In any other order a crew could be booked for a later job first and be missing for an earlier one.

The corridor jobs appear on two crews each (P012 on B and C, P020 on A and B), every crew's jobs are in sequence without overlap, and crew A takes the storm standby. The `assert` in the loop never fired. A model with named crews from the start (one optional interval per job and crew, as in lesson 4.5.1) would give the same answer with many more variables; when crews are interchangeable, schedule the pool and name the crews afterwards.
<!-- practice 3 -->
The Model
The season model `season_lateness.py` solves, in one place. Lesson 4.5.2 built the rules; this lesson added the due weeks, the lateness variables and the objective.
**Sets.** $`J`$ the jobs; $`O \subseteq J`$ the circuit clears; $`R`$ the regions, $`r(j)`$ the region of job $`j`$; $`\mathcal{W}_r`$ the outage windows of region $`r`$, each a span $`[a, b)`$.

**Parameters.** $`d_j`$, the weeks of job $`j`$; $`c_j`$, the crews it holds; $`\delta_j`$, its due week; $`w_j`$, its weight in $k per week late; $`K = 3`$ crews; $`H = 30`$ weeks; the standby, $`n = 1`$ crew away in weeks $`[12, 16)`$.
**Variables.**
**Objective.**
\min \; \sum_{j \in J} w_j\, L_j \qquad \leftarrow \text{this lesson}
**Constraints.**

rows: `add_cumulative(intervals, demands, crews)` with the standby interval

blocks.text: Summary

items: **Due weeks as hard rules make the season infeasible.** Five jobs due at week 6 need 36 crew-weeks against 18; a target that cannot always be met belongs in the objective.
**Lateness is max(0, end − due), and its weight is the risk carried.** `add_max_equality` with 0 in the list; minimize the weighted sum. The least-risk schedule carries $360k.
**The shortest season is not the safest one.** Both objectives give week 24; the makespan schedule carries $1,038k of risk. An objective optimizes what it says and nothing else.
**A checker written from the rules proves the schedule.** Plain Python, no shared code with the model, run on every schedule; test that it can fail.
**Named crews come from handing out free crews in start order.** The cumulative constraint guarantees the hand-out never runs short.

rows: ending the season early, whatever the order
fewer late weeks, every job alike
fewer late weeks where the risk is highest
as few late jobs as possible, however late they are

blocks.text: **Further reading:** OR-Tools, [The Job Shop Problem](https://developers.google.com/optimization/scheduling/job_shop) and [Employee Scheduling](https://developers.google.com/optimization/scheduling/employee_scheduling), the two models this module grew from; the CP-SAT samples [`cumulative_variable_profile_sample_sat.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/sat/samples/cumulative_variable_profile_sample_sat.py), whose `check_solution` re-computes the load minute by minute after the solve, the habit this lesson's checker follows, and [`ranking_sample_sat.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/sat/samples/ranking_sample_sat.py), which ranks the jobs on one resource with order literals, for when the order itself must be reported; the CP-SAT Primer, [Advanced Modeling](https://d-krupke.github.io/cpsat-primer/advanced_modelling.html), on intervals, presence literals and cumulative.
Challenges

items: Raise P006's weight to 30 in `season.py` and predict which job takes its place at the end of the season. Then run `season_lateness.py`.
Minimize the number of late jobs instead (one Boolean per job, as in the Reference table). Predict whether it is more or less than three, and what the risk-weighted lateness becomes.
In `crew_assignment.py`, hand out crews in order of job id instead of start week. Find the job for which the `assert` fires.

blocks.text: Design Note: Risk Weights Are a Model Too

The weights here are a crude proxy: consequence of failure over 100, flat for every week late. A real program would make the risk grow with the weeks (a tree grows into the line faster in midsummer) and with the circuit's condition. Two things carry over whatever the weights are. First, the objective is linear in the lateness, so a job's weight is exactly the price of one week's delay of that job, and a planner can read it that way. Second, the weights are data: keep them in the data set, next to the due weeks, where the asset-health team can review them, rather than in the model code. When they change, the schedule changes, and the checker still proves it keeps every rule.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**season_lateness.py.** The full season: due weeks as hard rules, then the makespan objective with its risk, then the least-risk schedule and the checker's verdict (*Due Weeks as Hard Rules Make the Season Infeasible*, *Lateness Is max(0, end − due)*, *The Shortest Season Is Not the Safest One*). *Try:* Remove the storm standby from `RULES`. Predict whether the least risk goes down, and by how much at most.
**check_demo.py.** The checker on the solver's schedule and on two hand edits (*A Checker Written From the Rules Proves the Schedule*). *Try:* Move P020 to week 12. Predict which rules break.

**crew_assignment.py.** Turns the least-risk pool schedule into named crews A, B and C (*Named Crews Come From Handing Out Free Crews in Start Order*). *Try:* Sort the free crews in reverse order. Predict whether the hand-out still succeeds.
**schedule_check.py.** The checker and the risk function, written from the rules with no solver. It runs nothing itself.
